fuller.text: This research paper introduces and tests dropout, a training trick for neural networks. Neural networks are programs built from many simple connected parts, called units, that learn patterns from examples. With limited training data, big networks often overfit: they learn quirks of the training examples that do not hold for new data. Dropout fights this by randomly switching off units, with their connections, while the network trains.

sentences.text: This research paper introduces and tests dropout, a training trick for neural networks.
Neural networks are programs built from many simple connected parts, called units, that learn patterns from examples.
With limited training data, big networks often overfit: they learn quirks of the training examples that do not hold for new data.
Dropout fights this by randomly switching off units, with their connections, while the network trains.

fuller.text: The authors note that averaging the answers of many different models nearly always helps. But training and running many large networks is too slow and costly, and there may not be enough data for each. Dropout offers a cheap stand-in: each switched-off pattern is a smaller "thinned" network, and all of them share the same connection strengths. A network with n units hides 2 to the power n such thinned networks, so training one network trains a huge family.

fuller.text: Each unit is kept with a chance p, often 0.5 for hidden units, which sit between input and output. For input units, the best chance of keeping one is usually closer to 1. At test time nothing is switched off; instead each unit's outgoing connection strengths, called weights, are multiplied by p. This makes each unit's output match its average output during training, roughly averaging all the thinned networks at once.

fuller.text: The idea comes partly from a theory of why sexual reproduction works: genes must be useful when mixed with random partners. Likewise, normal training lets units build fragile teamwork, called co-adaptation, where some units fix others' mistakes. Dropout makes partners unreliable, so each unit must learn something useful on its own.

fuller.text: On image tasks, dropout cut error rates, the share of wrong answers, every time. Handwritten digits (MNIST): error fell from about 1.60% to 0.95% with dropout and other tweaks, even in a network with 65 million settings. House numbers from street photos (SVHN): error fell from 3.95% to 2.55%. Small photos in 10 or 100 categories (CIFAR): error fell from 14.98% to 12.61%, and from 43.48% to 37.20%.

fuller.text: A dropout network won a large photo-recognition contest (ILSVRC-2012) with about 16% error, against about 26% for the best older methods. In speech recognition, error on identifying speech sounds fell from 23.4% to 21.8%. In sorting news articles by topic, the gain was smaller, from 31.05% to 29.62%.

fuller.text: Looking inside, units trained with dropout detected edges, strokes and spots, while units without it showed no clear meaning alone. Dropout did not help on tiny data sets of 100 or 500 examples; its benefit grew with more data, then shrank. The cheap test-time shortcut matched averaging about 50 randomly thinned networks.

fuller.text: The authors name clear limits. Dropout networks take 2 to 3 times longer to train, because each update is noisy. On a small genetics data set, slower Bayesian networks, which weight each model by how well it fits, still beat dropout.

fuller.text: The authors conclude that dropout is a general technique, not tied to any one field. Its core move is to take a large model that overfits easily and train many smaller sub-models sampled from it. They also extend it to other kinds of learning models, and call faster dropout a direction for future work.

brief.text: This paper presents dropout, a trick for training computer programs that learn from examples. Big learning programs often suffer from overfitting: they memorize quirks of their practice data, not general rules. Dropout fights this by randomly switching off parts of the program while it learns.

Dropout fights this by randomly switching off parts of the program while it learns.

brief.text: With no partner it can always lean on, each part must learn something useful on its own. In tests on pictures, speech, news articles and genetic data, dropout made the programs more accurate. The authors conclude it is a general method, not tied to one kind of task.
